summary: This RFC discusses security issues when variable bit rate audio is used with secure RTP, and suggests guidelines to reduce them. Packet sizes can reveal information even when the content is encrypted.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypting speech does not hide how long each packet is. A variable bit rate codec makes every packet match the words inside it, so the sizes alone give a clue to what was said. This document explains when that clue matters and how to remove it.

questions: packet length leaks in encrypted audio
does variable bit rate audio leak information in srtp
what is voice activity detection overhang
subtitle: Why the sizes of encrypted speech packets leak what was said, and how to make the leak too small to use.

tldr.problem: SRTP encrypts the payload of an RTP packet but adds no padding, so a variable bit rate codec produces packet sizes that follow the speech and leak a small amount of information about it.
tldr.mechanism: Use constant bit rate where the risk matters, add a random overhang period when using voice activity detection, and otherwise pad all packets to the same size with at least one octet of RTP padding.
tldr.outcome: Application designers get clear guidance on when variable bit rate audio is acceptable with SRTP and when it SHOULD NOT be used.

facts.label: Minimum padding
facts.value: At least one octet on all packets

facts.label: SRTP padding
facts.value: None of the predefined encryption transforms use padding

facts.label: What stays in the clear
facts.value: The RTP header and any header extension

sections.title: The Packet Size Leak
sections.content:
The Secure RTP (SRTP) framework, defined in RFC 3711, is a widely used framework for securing RTP sessions, as defined in RFC 3550. SRTP can encrypt the payload of an RTP packet and optionally add an authentication tag, while leaving the RTP header and any header extension in the clear. A range of encryption transforms can be used with SRTP, but none of the predefined encryption transforms use any padding, so the RTP and SRTP payload sizes match exactly.

When SRTP carries voice streams compressed with variable bit rate (VBR) codecs, the length of the compressed packets depends on the characteristics of the speech signal. That variation in packet size leaks a small amount of information about the contents of the speech signal, which is potentially a security risk for some applications. The RFC cites research showing that known phrases in an encrypted call using the Speex codec in VBR mode can be recognised with high accuracy in certain circumstances, and that approximate transcripts of encrypted VBR calls can be derived for some codecs without breaking the encryption. How significant these results are, and how they generalise to other codecs, is still an open question.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting the speech does not hide how long each packet is. A variable bit rate codec makes every packet match the words inside it, so the packet sizes describe what was said.

sections.title: Scenario-Dependent Risk
sections.content:
Whether the information leaks and the attacks described in the cited work are significant is highly dependent on the application and use scenario. In the worst case, using the rate information to recognise a prerecorded message while knowing the set of all possible messages would lead to near-perfect accuracy. Even when the audio is not prerecorded, there is a real possibility of recognising contents from encrypted audio when the dialogue is highly structured, for example when the eavesdropper knows that only a handful of possible sentences are possible and so the message contains only little information. Recognising unconstrained conversational speech from the rate information alone is unreliable and computationally expensive at present, but does appear possible in some circumstances. These attacks are only likely to improve over time.

In practical SRTP scenarios, the size of the information leak has to be weighed against other SRTP-related information that is already available, such as the source and destination IP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: How much a listener can learn depends on the situation. If there are only a few possible things to say, the packet sizes may be enough to tell them apart. For an open conversation, the sizes alone are much harder to read.

sections.title: Guidelines for Variable Bit Rate Audio
sections.content:
It is the responsibility of the application designer to determine the appropriate trade-off between security and bandwidth overhead. As a general rule, VBR codecs should be considered safe in the context of low-value encrypted unstructured calls. Applications that make use of prerecorded messages where the contents of such prerecorded messages may be of any value to an eavesdropper, that is, messages beyond standard greeting messages, SHOULD NOT use codecs in VBR mode. Interactive voice response (IVR) applications would be particularly vulnerable, since an eavesdropper could easily use the rate information to recognise the prompts being played out. Applications conveying highly sensitive unstructured information SHOULD NOT use codecs in VBR mode.

It is safe to use variable rate coding to adapt the output of a voice codec to the characteristics of a network channel, provided the adaptation is done in a way that does not expose any information on the speech signal. For example, VBR audio can be used for congestion control purposes, where the variation is driven by the available network bandwidth and not by the input speech, so the packet sizes and spacing stay constant unless the network conditions change. VBR speech codecs can safely be used in this fashion with SRTP while avoiding leaking information on the contents of the speech signal that might be useful for traffic analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Variable bit rate is fine for ordinary calls and for adapting to a busy network. It should not be used for recorded messages that an outsider would want to know, or for anything sensitive, because the packet sizes give the words away.

sections.title: Guidelines for Voice Activity Detection
sections.content:
Many speech codecs employ some form of voice activity detection (VAD) to either suppress output frames, or generate some form of lower-rate comfort noise frames, during periods when the speaker is not active. If VAD is used on an encrypted speech signal, some information about the characteristics of that speech signal can be determined by watching the patterns of voice activity. This information leakage is less than with VBR coding, since there are only two rates possible.

The information leakage due to VAD in SRTP audio sessions can be much reduced if the sender adds an unpredictable overhang period to the end of active speech intervals, obscuring their actual length. An RTP sender using VAD with encrypted SRTP audio SHOULD insert such an overhang period at the end of each talkspurt, delaying the start of the silence or comfort noise by a random interval. The length of the overhang applied to each talkspurt must be randomly chosen in such a way that it is computationally infeasible for an attacker to reliably estimate the length of that talkspurt. This may be more important for short talkspurts, since it seems easier to distinguish between different single word responses based on the exact word length than to glean meaning from the duration of a longer phrase. The audio data comprising the overhang period must be packetised and transmitted in RTP packets in a manner that is indistinguishable from the other data in the talkspurt.

The overhang period SHOULD have an exponentially decreasing probability distribution function. This ensures a long tail, while being easy to compute. It is RECOMMENDED to use an overhang with a half life of a few hundred milliseconds. This should be sufficient to obscure the presence of interword pauses and the lengths of single words spoken in isolation, for example the digits of a credit card number clearly enunciated for an automated system, but not so long as to significantly reduce the effectiveness of VAD for detecting listening pauses. Despite the overhang, and whatever its duration, there is still a small amount of information leaked about the start time of the talkspurt, because an overhang cannot be applied to the start of a talkspurt without unacceptably affecting intelligibility. For that reason, VAD SHOULD NOT be used in encrypted IVR applications where the content of prerecorded messages may be of any value to an eavesdropper.

The application of a random overhang period to each talkspurt will reduce the effectiveness of VAD in SRTP sessions when compared to non-SRTP sessions. However, it is still expected that the use of VAD will provide significant bandwidth savings for many encrypted sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: When the speaker stops, the codec often sends nothing, or sends quiet noise instead. A listener can see when the speaker stopped. The fix is to keep the line busy for a random extra time after each phrase, so the length of the phrase is hidden.

sections.title: Padding the Output of VBR Codecs
sections.content:
For scenarios where VBR is considered unsafe, a constant bit rate (CBR) codec SHOULD be negotiated and used instead, or the VBR codec SHOULD be operated in a CBR mode. However, if the codec does not support CBR, RTP padding SHOULD be used to reduce the information leak to an insignificant level. Packets may be padded to a constant size or to a small range of sizes; the cited research achieves good results by padding to the next multiple of 16 octets, though the amount of padding needed to hide the variation in packet size will depend on the codec and on the sophistication of the attacker. Packets may also be padded to a size that varies with time. The most secure and RECOMMENDED option is to pad all packets throughout the call to the same size.

In the case where the size of the padded packets varies in time, the same concerns as for VAD apply. The padding SHOULD NOT be reduced without waiting for a certain, random, time, and the RECOMMENDED hold time is the same as the one for VAD.

Note that SRTP encrypts the count of the number of octets of padding added to a packet, but not the bit in the RTP header that indicates that the packet has been padded. For this reason, it is RECOMMENDED to add at least one octet of padding to all packets in a media stream, so an attacker cannot tell which packets needed padding.
sections.plainLanguage: When variable bit rate is not acceptable, make every packet the same size. If the size has to change, change it only after a random delay. And pad every packet by at least one byte, so nobody can tell which packets were the short ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The entire document is about security, and the security considerations of RFC 3711 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole document is about security. The security rules of the SRTP specification itself still apply.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR THE RANDOM OVERHANG (RFC 6562, SECTION 4)

items.title: Delay the silence
items.text: Insert an overhang period at the end of each talkspurt, delaying the start of the silence or comfort noise by a random interval.

items.title: Choose it at random
items.text: The overhang length must be randomly chosen so that it is computationally infeasible to estimate the talkspurt length reliably.

items.title: Exponential distribution
items.text: The overhang period SHOULD have an exponentially decreasing probability distribution function, with a half life of a few hundred milliseconds.

items.title: Send it as speech
items.text: The overhang data must be packetised and transmitted in a manner indistinguishable from the other data in the talkspurt.

items.title: The start still leaks
items.text: A small amount of information remains about the start time of the talkspurt, so VAD SHOULD NOT be used in encrypted IVR applications.

items.title: Same size throughout
items.text: The most secure and RECOMMENDED option is to pad all packets throughout the call to the same size.

items.title: Rounded sizes
items.text: Packets may be padded to a small range of sizes, for example the next multiple of 16 octets.

items.title: Hold before shrinking
items.text: If the padded size varies over time, the padding SHOULD NOT be reduced without waiting for a random hold time, the same as the one used for VAD.

items.title: Always one octet
items.text: At least one octet of padding should be added to all packets, so an attacker cannot tell which packets needed padding.
